3.text: side by side on their haunches, looking into his face, he took it as a sign

4.text: that the time had come for him to withdraw from shamanistic practices. He

5.text: suffered a relapse of his illness, and his herd was visited by hoof-disease.

6.text: Fearing that worse things might happen, he dropped all serious pursuits of

7.text: shamanism, and practised only the tricks, which were completely harmless.

20.text: these wrong practices. “Look at my face,” he continued; “he who tells

24.text: Some of the people even are aware of the deceit of the shamans.

25.text: Several men, when talking of shamanistic feats, said that, though the tricks

26.text: performed were very wonderful, they were by no means real, but were pro-

27.text: duced only through illusion on the part of the observers. Others went even

28.text: further. Thus, the trader Kuvaˊr at Indian Point, of whom I have spoken

29.text: several times, assured me that even the most renowned shamans are only

30.text: clever deceivers. “When I witness their best trick,” he asserted, “even then,

31.text: with proper attention, I can discover the fraud. He [the shaman] will pretend

32.text: to cut with a knife the abdomen of the patient; but I can follow the direc-

33.text: tion of the knife, and see that it glances off without hurting the skin, and

34.text: that the blood comes from the mouth of the operator.”

35.text: This scepticism, perhaps, is the result of intercourse with civilized people.

36.text: With some of the shamans, fraud is not restricted to jugglery. We caught

37.text: Scratching-Woman in the very act of stealing our washing from the line.
